chapter: Home life and the father's death
title: Father's death in about 1907 and his strict teaching
summary: Tio places his father's death around 1907, explains why little is known of him compared with the uncle, and recalls his strict but gentle discipline over lessons; the conversation closes with chatter.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: When did your father die before I forget? I forgot to ask. About what year? If you don't remember exactly, you know, was it the time of the First World War or before? Must have been before that then. Alice. Oh, Alice. Yeah? Come here a minute please. Sorry to bother everybody. No, that's alright. These things are very interesting to us to do something like that.
Tell me something. How old were you when Papa died? Year and a half.
Year and a half.
Right. Now, this is urgent. What old are you now?
Fifty-four. That's why, alright. Fifty-four.
Fifty-four, so. Yeah. Now you see, he must have been dead.
I'll be fifty-five on the twenty-first day of January.
See, he's been dead now for... Fifty-three years.
That's right. That's right. That's right. Now, 1907 along in there then your father died. That's right. That's right. That's a long time ago, man. That's right.
That's right. Now, that's when he died.

That's another reason we don't hear as much about your father as we do your uncle, Lewis, because your uncle played a lot later than that, too, didn't he? Yeah, he did. He was playing with Fess, Professor Mineta, you know, in the... I'll excuse you. I'll excuse you. Yes, thank you very much.
I'm quite busy, thank you.
So, that's another reason we don't hear so much about him. He never lived long to play with the dance bands after 1907 and we wouldn't have... No, no, no, he didn't hear.

In other words, he played a lot of... He played several places, but the majority of the quality he did was... He wasn't writing. He did a lot of writing. Music writing. Because I remember when I was a kid, I was terrible, and he used to tell me, come here, son, go wash your hands, get yourself a drink of water, and get the music, get yourself a good lesson, and you got any school work to do, sit in that corner, and the doctor said you leave, kill me. And that was that, that was the law. Yeah. He never laid his hands on us, but that was... He just knew he meant business. That's right. That's what he meant. He meant you'd sit down there, and when you got away from me, you were very glad you could get out of there. And it made better... It made better cheering, I think, than it do today.
I believe so, too. By the way, are we holding up your dinner? No, no, no. Keeping you from dinner?

I think we don't... No, no. No. Well, as I said, after he found out that all the segregation and things was coming on, he decided to leave. And I guess, had he lived, he never would have been here. Probably would have come back here.
Did he die in Bay St. Louis, then? No, he died here. He came back at the beach, then? Yeah, we brought him here.
He died here. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you. Well, gentlemen.
